messages.subject: modeling spatial structure in HMs
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Apologies for shameless self-PR here, but I think here’s a paper of some general (methodological) interest because it shows how spatial structure can easily be incorporated in HMs of the kinds that we talk about on this list. My colleagues had an observational study with a split-plot design: where there are nested levels of observation, with some covariates measured on one level and some on another. Just ignoring this inherent dependency would be bad (e.g., “pseudoreplication” and all that). The traditional way in mixed-model and ANOVA land to accommodate such spatial structure is to fit a random block effect to account for increased similarity of plots within the same block as opposed to those lying in different blocks. This is of course easily achieved in BUGS and here is an example inside of an abundance-based community model (i.e., a DRY model according to Chapter 11 in AHM1).

To view the online publication, please click here:

http://journal.frontiersin.org/article/10.3389/fevo.2018.00175/full?&utm_source=Email_to_authors_&utm_medium=Email&utm_content=T1_11.5e1_author&utm_campaign=Email_publication&field=&journalName=Frontiers_in_Ecology_and_Evolution&id=349063

Of course, we’re not the first ones to do this, e.g., David Miller has a paper around 2013 where they accommodate such a blocking structure in a single-species occupancy model (I believe) and no doubt there must be others. But my point here is just to (1) emphasize that often we have such internal structure that is induced by the design of our study and (2) we can easily account for the resulting spatial structure.

Bestr regards  --- Marc

messages.subject: RE: modeling spatial structure in HMs
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

motivated by an email from Jerry Cole, I would like to add the following:

Blocking is really only the crudest form of accounting for similarity due to spatial proximity. On the other end of the spectrum are geostatistical models, such as these (in the context of 'interesting' HMs):
https://www.researchgate.net/publication/51171238_Using_multilevel_spatial_models_to_understand_salamander_site_occupancy_patterns_after_wildfire

CAR models and geostatistical models with negative exponential correlation function can be fit with functions in WinBUGS or OpenBUGS, but not JAGS (you'd have to code them up yourself).

With BUGS, splines are much more efficient though, see for instance here in the context of a static occupancy model:  https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/j.1472-4642.2011.00831.x

If you are worried that blocking doesn't remove all the residual spatial autocorrelation, you could conceivably combine block effects (to eliminate larger-scale heterogeneity) with such more fine-scale modeling of residual correlations in the same model.

Finally, it's worth mentioning some R packages that can do (static) occupancy or Nmix models with modeling of residual spatial autocorrelation:
- For static occupancy models, there is the stocc R package, which does them with CAR and RSR, see  https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1890/12-0564.1
- For static occupancy and Nmix models, there is the the hSDM package: https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/hSDM/hSDM.pdf

Best regards  ---- Marc

messages.subject: Re: modeling spatial structure in HMs
messages.body_plain:
Thanks for the info and links Marc. I’ll just also note a recent paper of ours (shameless plug) where we included spatially-explicit random effects (essentially continuous without blocking) in a hierarchical abundance model: https://esajournals.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/eap.1767

We did it in a frequentist framework rather than Bayesian for practical purposes using TMB, which employs fast automatic differentiation. Our simulations and analyses are specific to stream networks but the same approach could be employed for 2D space using Gaussian Markov Random Fields with a triangulation mesh and Matern correlation function with distance. This is a similar approach to INLA (which package can still be used to create the mesh). With INLA it’s difficult to get the hierarchical structure of the N-mixture or occupancy model and include other hierarchical information (see Meehan’s recent work: https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.01581 ).

Our approach works for static abundance models but also with timing varying (currently AR1) and modeling varying spatiotemporally but the spatiotemporal requires a lot of data over many years based on our basic simulations.

Cheers,
Dan

messages.subject: Comparison of HDS in unmarked and JAGS
messages.subject_clean: Comparison of HDS in unmarked and JAGS
messages.body_plain:
Hi folks

I'm trying to compare results from fitting a hierarchical distance sampling model with the unmarked package and a Bayesian implementation using JAGS.  I successfully fit a basic single-occasion HDS model with a half-normal detection function and negative binomial abundance model using the gdistsamp function in unmarked. However, when I fitted a Bayesian version in JAGS, I ran into trouble with estimating sigma for the detection function. Essentially, the posterior continually pushed up against the upper bound of the uniform prior as I incrementally increased that bound which basically caused detection to be 1 at all feasible distances and the abundance estimates to equal the raw counts. My guess is that I have some inherent mis-specification in my JAGS model statement that I am unable to see. Perhaps someone else out there can spot the problem. My test is based on real data that I would be willing to share offline if necessary. In short, the data contains too many transects with zero counts to fit a Poisson abundance model, hence the negative binomial. The transect half-width is 300 m and distance bins are 50 m. Perfect detection can safely be assumed at distance 0. The detection parameter estimates from the unmarked analysis do result in a detection function that aligns with field expectations and similar studies on the same taxon. Note that I have already tried using estimates from the unmarked analysis as starting values for the JAGS analysis. No bueno. Any insights would be greatly appreciated. Below is the JAGS model statement and calls to the requisite unmarked functions to fit the likelihood version.

Cheers!
Jared

cat("
    model{
        ## priors
        beta0 ~ dnorm(0,0.01)
        r ~ dunif(0,upperr)
        sigma ~ dunif(0,500)
        ## derive psi
        psi <- sum(Ng[])/(ngroups+nz)
        ## detection model
        for(i in 1:(ngroups+nz)){
            z[i] ~ dbern(psi) # data augmentation model
            bindist[i] ~ dcat(pi[]) # distance distribution (prior)
            mu.p[i] <- z[i]*exp(-bindist[i]*bindist[i]/(2*sigma*sigma)) # detection function
            y[i] ~ dbern(mu.p[i])
            transect[i] ~ dcat(transect.probs[1:ntransects]) # multinomial for transect membership
        }
        ##
        for(s in 1:ntransects){
            ## population model
            Ng[s] ~ dnegbin(p[s],r) # transect-level abundance
            log(mu.nb[s]) <- beta0
            p[s] <- r/(mu.nb[s] + r)
            transect.probs[s] <- Ng[s]/sum(Ng[]) # probability vector for multinomial
        }
        ##
        ## derived quantities
        G <- sum(z[]) # total population abundance across transects
    }
    ",fill=TRUE, file="model0.jags")

binw <- 50
gdf <- unmarkedFrameGDS(y=data,
                        siteCovs=siteCovs,
                        numPrimary=1,
                        dist.breaks=c(0,seq(binw,300-binw,binw),300),
                        survey="line",
                        unitsIn="m",
                        tlength=yy$length*1000)
gout <- gdistsamp(lambdaformula=~1,
                  phiformula=~1,
                  pformula=~1,
                  data=gdf,
                  keyfun="halfnorm",
                  output="abund",
                  unitsOut="kmsq",
                  mixture="NB")
